papers.partial_detail: Read in full: abstract, Sections 1-4 (introduction, preliminaries, zero-one loss results including Lemma 1, Theorem 2, Lemma 3 and proofs, Corollary 5, Remark 6, Corollary 7 statement, Proposition 8 with proof, Theorem 9, Remarks 10-11, Corollary 12, Remark 13) and Section 8 (conclusions). Skimmed by keyword search only: Appendix A.3-A.5 (Corollary 7 proofs, Le Cam and Assouad derivations, divergence comparison; A.4 two-point part read). Not read: Sections 5-7 (f-informativity upper bounds, Gaussian location example, Gaussian mixtures, sparse regression) and Appendices B-C. Keyword search for binary, skew, imbalance, rare and non-uniform found only the uniform binary example in Remark 6, the Le Cam two-point case with prior 1/2 each, and a binary-testing reduction with uniform labels.
papers.what_it_is: A JMLR paper that proves Bayes risk lower bounds for arbitrary priors and losses using f-informativity and the data processing inequality, including a generalized Fano inequality for any prior with zero-one loss.
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: Journal of Machine Learning Research 17 (2016) 1-58 Submitted 4/16; Revised 10/16; Published 12/16

assertions.value: For any prior w and any zero-one valued loss L, R_Bayes(w,L) >= 1 + (I(w,P) + log(1+R0)) / log(sup_a w(B(a))), where B(a) = {theta : L(theta,a) = 0}, I(w,P) is the mutual information between theta ~ w and X, and R0 is the no-data Bayes risk. Printed denominator is log of the largest prior mass of any ball B(a); the proof shows it equals log(1 - R0). No assumptions on the parameter space, action space or prior.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.1, Corollary 5, eq (25), p. 13; stated in Section 1.1, eq (5), p. 3

we give an affirmative answer by proving that inequality (5) holds for any zero-one valued loss function L and any prior w.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved theorem in a peer-reviewed journal (JMLR 17, 2016); the statement is general with no extra conditions beyond zero-one loss and R0 > 0. Formula read from the extracted text; the proof's intermediate form with log(1 - R0) is consistent with it.

assertions.value: R0 is the infimum over actions a of the prior-expected loss, with a not depending on the data: the Bayes risk of the no-data problem. For zero-one loss, R0 = 1 - sup_a w(B(a)), one minus the largest prior mass of any single ball B(a).
quotes: Note that R0 represents the Bayes risk with respect to w in the "no data" problem i.e., when one only has information on
the quantity R0 has the following alternative expression:
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in the paper; the alternative expression (15) follows directly for zero-one loss.

assertions.value: The Bayes risk never exceeds R0 (0 <= R_Bayes <= R0), so R_Bayes = 0 when R0 = 0. The paper therefore assumes R0 > 0 throughout Section 3.
quotes: the risk with some data cannot be greater than the risk in the no data problem
We shall therefore assume throughout this section that R0 > 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Elementary argument given in the text (constant decision rules are a subset of all rules).

assertions.value: Theorem 2: for zero-one loss and any convex f with f(1)=0, I_f(w,P) >= phi_f(R_Bayes(w), R0), where phi_f(a,b) is the f-divergence between two-point distributions on {0,1} with P{1}=a and Q{1}=b. Since phi_f(r,R0) is non-increasing in r on [0,R0], this gives an implicit lower bound R_Bayes >= g^{-1}(I_f), with g(r) = phi_f(r,R0).
quotes: The only assumption is that L is zero-one valued and we do not assume the existence of the Bayes decision rule.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved theorem in a peer-reviewed journal (JMLR 17, 2016); the statement is general with no extra conditions beyond zero-one loss and R0 > 0.

assertions.value: The f-informativity is I_f(w,P) = inf over probability measures Q on the sample space of the w-average of D_f(P_theta || Q). For f(x) = x log x (KL divergence) it equals the mutual information I(w,P).
quotes: is equal to the mutual information and is denoted by I(w, P).

assertions.value: Corollary 5 is slightly stronger than the form (5) with log 2 in the numerator, because R0 <= 1 gives log(1+R0) <= log 2. Example in the paper: parameter and action set {0,1}, indicator loss, prior 1/2 each, so R0 = 1/2; form (5) gives a trivial (negative) bound, while (25) still gives a useful bound whenever I(w,P) < log 2 - log(3/2).
quotes: the inequality (25) still provides a useful lower bound when
assertions.certainty_reason: Elementary comparison of the two forms; the numeric example is stated by the authors and checks against (25) with R0 = 1/2.

assertions.value: The classical Fano inequality (uniform prior on N points, indicator loss) and the continuum Fano inequality of Duchi and Wainwright (2013) are both special cases of (5), hence of Corollary 5, restricted to uniform priors. In the finite uniform setting w(B(a)) = 1/N, so R0 = 1 - 1/N.
quotes: Indeed, both these inequalities are special instances of the following inequality:
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors with a short derivation; the paper does not discuss any non-uniform special case.

assertions.value: For zero-one loss and any prior, other f-divergences give explicit bounds in terms of R0: with chi-squared informativity R >= R0 - R0(1-R0) I_2(w,P); with total variation informativity R >= R0 - I_TV(w,P). The paper states the choice of f-divergence affects tightness, and that KL and chi-squared bounds are much stronger than Hellinger in the discrete uniform setting.
quotes: divergence will affect the tightness of the lower bound for R.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved theorem in a peer-reviewed journal (JMLR 17, 2016); the statement is general with no extra conditions beyond zero-one loss and R0 > 0. The formulas are as read from the extracted text; the proofs are in Appendix A.3, which was not read.

assertions.value: The general-loss bound (Theorem 9, Corollary 12) may not be tight for priors with spikes, because it involves sup_a w(B_t(a,L)), which becomes large when the prior has extremely large density in a small region. The authors say tight bounds in this generality are an open problem, and that bounds are not always tight because of the generality. The paper gives a partitioning fix (Remark 11) for densities bounded above.
quotes: Because of the generality, the bounds are not always tight however.
In such situations, our main Bayes risk lower bound in Theorem 9 will not be tight.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limitation stated by the authors. It is stated for Theorem 9 (general loss); the paper does not say whether it also affects Corollary 5 for a skewed binary prior.

methods.name: Generalized Fano inequality (Corollary 5)
methods.what_it_bounds: Lower bound on the Bayes risk R_Bayes(w,L) for zero-one loss under an arbitrary prior w.
methods.inputs_needed: An upper bound on the mutual information I(w,P) between parameter and data; R0 = 1 - sup_a w(B(a)), computable from the prior and loss alone.
methods.fails_when: The paper states no conditions beyond zero-one loss and R0 > 0. The bound is trivial (<= 0) when I(w,P) is large relative to the prior-mass terms. The paper does not discuss skewed or binary non-uniform priors.
